items.title: Ask HN: How long before someone reverse-engineers Windows?
items.summary: It just occurred to me that similar to Photoshop suite, someone is already working on getting Windows 10/11 reverse-engineered in a clean-room fashion. I don't want to get into the discussion over the whole Craft suite, it's already been the talk of past week, after all, but judging by the pure popularity and the number of merge requests created within those couple days for just their Photoshop equivalent app, I am guessing these projects are not* going away anytime soon and they will, in fact, polish-out majority of issues: https://github.com/storytold/photocraft/pulls Also, while the original authors claim it was done without the debugger, I am absolutely certain thousands have their LLMs actively analyzing Adobe Suite now to get understand the knicks and crannies of it. So if people hating on Adobe flocked to contribute to this project so enthusiastically, I guess we can only imagine the sheer amount of interest worldwide an open-source Windows would bring, and not only from the volunteers this time around..

Show HN: Parsimony – an open-source benchmark for how much code AI models add
items.summary: Existing benchmarks measure solve rate and token output/cost, but don't punish excess code, which makes a codebase harder to work with in the long term. I wanted to measure this since it matters most for long-term projects. Method: it takes the patches that benchmarks already publish (DeepSWE, SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Live) and counts "coding units": syntax elements like statements, calls, names and literals. I didn't use lines of code, so cramming code isn't rewarded. Deleted code is subtracted, so it measures net units. GPT-6 and Claude 5.5 have no public patches yet, so I ran them myself on 3–10 tasks on my own subscriptions (shown as faded circles, not ranked). Any feedback or model contributions are welcome, especially public patch exports for newer models. GitHub: https://github.com/La5u/Parsimony Not affiliated with any of the benchmarks.

items.title: Show HN: Hatoba, an open-source SSH client with an AI assistant and E2EE sync
items.summary: I've used SSH tools for years and didn't really plan on building yet another SSH client, but I ended up building one the way I wanted. Hatoba is a desktop SSH client for Windows, Linux and macOS. It's written in Rust with Tauri 2 and MIT licensed. Each terminal has an AI assistant panel next to it. You describe the problem, and it reads the terminal screen, runs commands, types into the shell, and reads, edits and searches files on the host to find the cause and fix it. You can approve every command and edit it before it runs, let a model you pick approve the safe ones, or turn approval off. Files it changes show a diff you can undo. It works with any OpenAI-compatible or Anthropic API, local models included, and supports skills and MCP servers. Sync doesn't go through a server of mine. Hatoba deploys a Worker and a D1 database to your own Cloudflare account and syncs hosts, keys and AI conversations through them. The free plan usually covers personal use. Everything is encrypted on the device before it leaves. Keys are derived from your master password with Argon2id, every item is encrypted with AES-256-GCM, and the Worker only stores ciphertext plus the hashes it needs to sign you in. Someone who gets hold of the whole Cloudflare account still only gets ciphertext. Sync is optional, and everything works offline without it. The usual SSH client features are there too: groups, tags and fuzzy search, ~/.ssh/config import, ProxyJump and SOCKS5/HTTP proxies, an SFTP panel, local port forwarding, and a key vault that imports OpenSSH, PEM and PuTTY keys. There's also a dashboard showing CPU, memory, disk and network for every saved host, read over plain SSH with nothing installed on the servers. SSH is russh, the terminal is xterm.js with the WebGL renderer, and the UI is React. I develop on Windows, so it's Windows first, with a custom title bar that supports Snap Layouts and Mica, and working CJK input methods. The Linux packages and the macOS build get far less testing on real machines. The macOS build is Apple Silicon only and isn't notarized, so macOS blocks it on first launch until you allow it in Privacy & Security. Bug reports from Linux and Mac users would help the most. Website: https://hatoba.fog.moe Downloads: https://hatoba.fog.moe/download/
